meta.audience: His brethren, the Jews, and all the ends of the earth

world_behind.title: The last chapter of a long book
world_behind.text: Two books, fifty-five chapters, and this is Nephi's goodbye. He is old, the plates are nearly full, and everything in these fifteen verses is chosen under that pressure. It is also the only place he assesses his own writing.

world_behind.title: Speaking versus engraving
world_behind.text: Verse 1 draws a distinction the record's other writers will repeat: when a man speaks by the Holy Ghost the power carries it to the hearts of men, but writing is harder. Engraving on metal is slow, unrevisable, and silent, and Nephi names that as a real limitation rather than a modest formula.

world_behind.title: A handover, not just a goodbye
world_behind.text: The next book opens with Nephi giving the plates to Jacob and commanding him what to write. This farewell is therefore also an administrative act: the record changes hands immediately after it, and Jacob's first chapter refers back to instructions given at this moment.

world_behind.title: All ye ends of the earth
world_behind.text: The phrase appears twice in these fifteen verses, in the two places where Nephi widens his address past his own people. It is the largest audience formula the record has, and he reaches for it in a farewell rather than in a prophecy.

world_behind.title: Nothing about the reign
world_behind.text: Nephi ruled a colony, built a temple, made swords, and was called their king in all but name. None of it appears here. His closing account of himself is entirely about writing, praying, and believing, which is a striking selection for a man with a public life to summarize.

world_behind.title: Two farewells, not one
world_behind.text: Verse 13 says farewell until the great day to those who will hear; verse 14 bids an everlasting farewell to those who will not. Nephi divides his audience at the end and speaks to both halves in consecutive verses.

words.text: To be brought back into agreement after a breach, and the verb assumes the breach is real. Nephi makes it the first of four conditions on which his hope for anyone rests, ahead of the gate, the path, and enduring. Jacob had used the same word for the same act three chapters into his sermon, and it is the record's standard term for the human side of the atonement.

To take a share of something offered. The everlasting farewell is addressed to those who will not partake of the goodness of God, which locates the refusal at a table rather than at an argument. Nothing in the verse says they disbelieved; it says they declined a portion.

phrases.term: neither am I mighty in writing, like unto speaking
phrases.text: The record's first statement of an anxiety that later writers repeat at length. The reason given is specific: spoken words carried by the Holy Ghost go to the hearts of men, and writing lacks that delivery. Moroni will make the same complaint about the same plates, so the worry outlives Nephi by a thousand years.

phrases.term: esteem them as things of naught
phrases.text: To esteem is to value, to reckon at a price, and the word appears twice in two verses with opposite subjects: they esteem the writings as nothing, and Nephi esteems them as of great worth. The failure is located in hardened hearts rather than in the text. People whose hearts leave no place for the Spirit discard what is written, and the verse describes it as an act of valuation. Nothing here suggests the objectors have found an error; they have simply priced the thing at nothing.

phrases.term: mine eyes water my pillow by night
phrases.text: One of the few physical details Nephi gives about his own life, and it is placed inside a sentence about praying continually for his people. He does not say what he weeps about. The verse sits between his high estimate of his writing and his confidence that God will consecrate his prayers.

phrases.term: written in weakness will be made strong
phrases.text: The chapter's answer to verse 1. He does not withdraw the complaint; he says God will compensate for it, and then lists what the words will do: persuade to do good, make known the fathers, speak of Jesus. Moroni will be told the same thing in nearly the same terms when he raises the same worry.

To glory in something is to boast in it, to make it the ground of one's standing, and the verb is used three times in one line: plainness, truth, and then a person. The possessive is the striking part. Nephi has spent two books using titles, Messiah, Redeemer, Holy One of Israel, Lamb of God, and in his final testimony he says my Jesus. It is the most personal sentence in his writing, and it is placed between plainness and truth, as though it belonged to the same list.

phrases.term: I have charity for the Jew
phrases.text: He says it and immediately explains the word, "I say Jew, because I mean them from whence I came" (v. 8). The aside is unnecessary for his own people and necessary for later readers, which suggests who he thinks is holding the plates. Charity for the Gentiles follows in the next verse, with a condition attached to both.

cites.quote: I say Jew, because I mean them from whence I came

spans.text: I say Jew, because I mean them from whence I came

phrases.term: believe in Christ, and believe these words
phrases.text: The test he leaves. Not that believing his words proves Christ, but that believing Christ will lead a reader to accept these words, because they are Christ's. The logic runs from the person to the text rather than the other way, which is the same order chapter 11 used for Isaiah.

phrases.term: the voice of one crying from the dust
phrases.text: Isaiah's figure of a fallen people whose "speech shall be low out of the dust" (Isa. 29:4), applied by Nephi to the record two chapters into his commentary and now to himself. He is alive when he writes it. The farewell is spoken in the voice of a man already counting himself among the buried.

phrases.term: what I seal on earth, shall be brought against you
phrases.text: To seal is a legal act, closing a document so it can be opened only by authority, and the word ties this farewell to the sealed book of chapter 27. The last sentence of two books, and it is a legal deposit rather than a blessing. Nephi adds that the Lord commanded it and that he must obey, which frames even the severity as obedience. The record's readers are told, in the final verse, that they are parties to a case.

verses.label: v. 1–2
verses.title: A writer's honest assessment
verses.text: He cannot write everything, he is not mighty in writing, and the reason is that spoken words carried by the Spirit reach hearts in a way engraving does not. Then the other half: some people harden their hearts and discard what is written. Both the medium and the audience are named as obstacles.

verses.label: v. 3–4
verses.title: High worth, and tears
verses.text: Against the low estimate of his skill he sets a high estimate of his work: great worth, especially to his people. Then prayer, a wet pillow, and confidence that God will consecrate the prayers and strengthen the words. The two verses hold weakness and assurance without resolving them into either.

verses.label: v. 5–6
verses.title: Plainness, and one possessive
verses.text: The words speak harshly against sin, so anger at them indicates a spirit rather than a disagreement. Then the three gloryings, ending in my Jesus. After fifty-five chapters of careful titles, the possessive arrives without preparation.

verses.label: v. 7–9
verses.title: Affection, and its terms
verses.text: For his people, for the Jews, for the Gentiles. The definition of Jew is supplied for a reader who would not know it. Then the condition that applies to all three: reconciled to Christ, in at the narrow gate, walking the strait path, enduring. Charity does not soften the terms.

verses.label: v. 10–11
verses.title: The test he leaves
verses.text: Believe in Christ, and if you do not believe these words, believe in Christ; if you believe in Christ you will believe these words. Then the alternative: judge for yourselves, and Christ will show you at the last day, when writer and reader stand face to face.

verses.label: v. 12–13
verses.title: A prayer, and goodbye
verses.text: He prays that many, if not all, may be saved, and then says goodbye until the great day. The qualifier in verse 12 is characteristic of him, hopeful and exact at once, and it is the last thing he asks for.

verses.label: v. 14–15
verses.title: The everlasting farewell
verses.text: To those who will not partake of the goodness of God, a different goodbye and a sealed record brought against them at the bar. The book ends on obedience rather than on triumph: thus hath the Lord commanded me, and I must obey.

chapter.title: The book ends with its author unsure of his medium
chapter.text: Nephi's last chapter opens by saying he is not mighty in writing. Whatever confidence he claimed in chapter 25 about plainness that no man could err in, the final assessment is more modest, and it is the one his successors quote.

chapter.title: Weakness and worth are held together
chapter.text: Verse 1 and verse 3 sit two sentences apart: not mighty in writing, and of great worth. He does not resolve the tension by claiming skill or by dismissing the work. God making weak writing strong is the only bridge offered.

chapter.title: Charity comes with terms
chapter.text: Three groups are named and one condition applies to all: reconciliation, the gate, the path, enduring. The chapter refuses to let affection stand in for agreement about what is required, which is consistent with the two chapters before it.

chapter.title: The reader is addressed as a future party
chapter.text: Face to face at his bar, sealed words brought against them, a farewell divided by response. Nephi writes as though the person holding the plates is in the room, and the last verse makes that literal.

chapter.title: Isaiah's dust returns, personally
chapter.text: The figure was applied to the record, then to the destroyed people, and finally to himself as he says goodbye. Across three chapters the same image moves from a prophecy about a book to a living man's description of his own voice.

chapter.title: The unit closes as it opened
chapter.text: Chapter 31 named the doctrine and the gate; chapter 33 names the same gate and path in verse 9 as the condition of his hope for anyone. Nephi's last argument is the one he made first, and the farewell adds only that he will be there when it is settled.

applications.title: Write it anyway
applications.text: Nephi thought he was bad at writing and wrote two books. Whatever you have been putting off recording — a testimony, a family history, a letter — do it in the weakness you actually have, on the chapter's own promise about what God does with weak writing.

applications.title: Check your appraisal
applications.text: The chapter's failure mode is pricing something at nothing. Name a source of counsel you have quietly written off, and ask whether you evaluated it or simply stopped valuing it.

applications.title: Say the possessive
applications.text: Nephi spent two books on titles and ended with "my Jesus." Try saying it that way once, in prayer, and notice whether it is easy or difficult, and why.

applications.title: Extend charity with the terms intact
applications.text: Think of someone you disagree with about what discipleship requires. Practice holding genuine affection for them and the actual requirement at the same time, without softening either.

applications.title: Run the verse 10 test
applications.text: When you doubt a scripture, try the order Nephi gives: start from Christ rather than from the text, and see whether the text follows. The logic runs person first, words second.

applications.title: Draft your own last paragraph
applications.text: Draft what you would want to say to the people who will read your record. It clarifies, quickly, what you actually believe is worth passing on.

questions.text: What do I avoid doing because I am not good at it, and who is not being reached as a result?
What do I water my pillow over, and do I pray about the same thing?
Could I honestly say "my Jesus," or is the relationship more formal than that?
Who are "them from whence I came," and do I have charity for them?
If I stood face to face with a writer of scripture, which of my objections would I still want to make?
What would be brought against me from what I have sealed by my own life?
